# 1 Samuel Chapter 25 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 164v–165v | **Source Image:** 1SA_025_page_001.jpg, 1SA_025_page_002.jpg, 1SA_025_page_003.jpg

---

**1** Samuel died, and all Israel gathered to mourn him. They buried him at his home in Ramah. Then David moved down to the Wilderness of Paran.

**2** There was a man in Maon whose business was in Carmel. He was very wealthy — three thousand sheep and a thousand goats — and he was shearing his sheep in Carmel.

**3** His name was Nabal, and his wife's name was Abigail. She was intelligent and beautiful. He was harsh and mean in his dealings — a Calebite.

**4** While in the wilderness, David heard that Nabal was shearing his sheep.

**5** He sent ten young men, telling them, "Go up to Carmel, find Nabal, and greet him in my name.

**6** Say to him: 'Long life to you! Peace to you, peace to your household, and peace to everything that is yours.

**7** I hear that you are shearing. When your shepherds were with us, we never mistreated them, and nothing of theirs went missing the whole time they were in Carmel.

**8** Ask your own servants — they will tell you. So show my young men some kindness, since we come on a festive day. Please give whatever you can spare to your servants and to your son David.'"

**9** David's young men went and delivered the message to Nabal word for word, and then waited.

**10** Nabal answered David's servants, "Who is David? Who is this son of Jesse? The countryside is full of slaves running away from their masters these days.

**11** Why should I take my bread, my water, and the meat I have butchered for my shearers and give it to men who come from who knows where?"

**12** David's young men turned around and went back, and they reported every word.

**13** David said to his men, "Strap on your swords!" Every man strapped on his sword, and David strapped on his. About four hundred men marched out with David, while two hundred stayed behind with the supplies.

**14** Meanwhile, one of Nabal's servants told Abigail, "David sent messengers from the wilderness to pay our master his respects, and he flew into a rage at them.

**15** But those men were very good to us. We were never harassed, and we never lost a thing the whole time we were out in the fields with them.

**16** They were like a wall around us, night and day, the entire time we were with them tending the flocks.

**17** Think carefully about what you should do, because disaster is hanging over our master and his whole household. He is so worthless that no one can even talk to him."

**18** Abigail wasted no time. She gathered two hundred loaves of bread, two skins of wine, five dressed sheep, five measures of roasted grain, a hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of pressed figs, and loaded them on donkeys.

**19** She told her servants, "Go on ahead of me. I will be right behind you." But she said nothing to her husband Nabal.

**20** As she was riding her donkey down a mountain ravine, David and his men were coming toward her — and she met them head on.

**21** David had been saying to himself, "I guarded everything this man owns in the wilderness for nothing! Not one thing of his went missing — and he has paid me back evil for good.

**22** May God strike David's enemies dead if by morning I leave alive a single male in his household!"

**23** When Abigail saw David, she quickly got off her donkey, fell on her face before him, and bowed to the ground.

**24** She fell at his feet and said, "Let the blame fall on me, my lord. Please, let your servant speak, and hear what I have to say.

**25** My lord should pay no attention to that worthless man Nabal. He is exactly what his name says — 'Fool' is his name, and foolishness follows him everywhere. As for me, your servant, I never saw the young men you sent.

**26** Now, my lord — as surely as the LORD lives and as you yourself live — the LORD has held you back from bloodshed and from taking justice into your own hands. May your enemies and all who seek to harm you end up like Nabal.

**27** And now, please accept this gift that your servant has brought for my lord. Let it be given to the young men who follow you.

**28** Please forgive your servant's boldness. The LORD will certainly establish a lasting dynasty for my lord, because my lord fights the LORD's battles, and no wrongdoing will ever be found in you throughout your life.

**29** Even if someone rises up to pursue you and seek your life, my lord's life will be held secure in the bundle of the living by the LORD your God, while the lives of your enemies he will hurl away like stones from a sling.

**30** When the LORD has done for my lord everything good he has promised, and has appointed you ruler over Israel,

**31** then you will not have this weighing on your conscience — this stain on your heart — that you shed innocent blood or took vengeance into your own hands. And when the LORD has blessed my lord, remember your servant."

**32** David said to Abigail, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you to meet me today!

**33** Blessed is your good judgment, and blessed are you for keeping me today from bloodshed and from taking vengeance with my own hands.

**34** As surely as the LORD God of Israel lives — the one who held me back from harming you — if you had not hurried out to meet me, not a single male in Nabal's household would have been left alive by morning."

**35** David accepted from her hand what she had brought and said to her, "Go home in peace. See, I have listened to what you said and granted your request."

**36** When Abigail came home to Nabal, he was holding a feast fit for a king. Nabal was in high spirits and very drunk, so she told him nothing at all until morning.

**37** In the morning, when the wine had worn off, his wife told him everything. His heart failed within him and he became like a stone.

**38** About ten days later, the LORD struck Nabal, and he died.

**39** When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, "Blessed be the LORD, who has upheld my cause against Nabal's insult and kept his servant from doing wrong. The LORD has brought Nabal's evil down on his own head." Then David sent word to Abigail, proposing marriage.

**40** David's servants went to Abigail at Carmel and told her, "David has sent us to you to take you as his wife."

**41** She rose, bowed with her face to the ground, and said, "Your servant is ready — even to wash the feet of my lord's servants."

**42** Abigail quickly mounted her donkey, and with five of her young women attending her, she followed David's messengers and became his wife.

**43** David also married Ahinoam of Jezreel, so both women became his wives.

**44** Saul, meanwhile, had given his daughter Michal — David's wife — to Palti son of Laish, who was from Gallim.

---

## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

Chapter 25 is the narrative hinge between the two cave/sparing episodes (chs. 24 and 26), and its placement is deliberate. David, who just swore not to take revenge on Saul, nearly massacres an entire household over an insult. The chapter probes the limits of David's restraint when the offender is not the LORD's anointed but merely a wealthy fool.

Samuel's death in v. 1 is reported in a single sentence — terse, monumental, final. Israel mourns. David moves on. The juxtaposition is the narrator's way of signaling that Israel is now in the wilderness between prophetic eras.

Nabal's name (*naval*, "fool") is too perfect to be accidental; the narrator likely uses it as a literary device. Abigail herself calls attention to it in v. 25 with a wordplay that is untranslatable in its full force: *ki khishmo ken hu — Naval shemo unevalah immo* ("as his name is, so is he — Fool is his name and folly is with him"). The dynamic rendering aims for the same punchy directness.

Abigail's speech (vv. 24-31) is the longest and most theologically sophisticated speech by a woman in the Books of Samuel. She argues not merely for mercy but for David's political future: bloodshed now would become a "stumbling block of heart" (*mikshol lev*) when he is king. The image in v. 29 — the soul "bound in the bundle of the living" (*tzeror hachayim*) — is one of the Hebrew Bible's most beautiful metaphors for divine protection, later adopted in Jewish memorial liturgy. The contrasting image of enemies slung away like stones from a sling (*betokh kaf haqela*) is grimly apt for the man who killed Goliath.

David's oath in v. 22 contains a scribal euphemism (*tiqqun soferim*): the Leningrad Codex reads "enemies of David" where the original likely read "David" himself, avoiding the curse falling on Israel's future king.

— PNEUMA
